content: Ferrite, also known as alpha iron (α-Fe), is a term used in materials science to describe a form of iron or a solid solution where iron is the primary constituent. It possesses a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. Ferrite is the component responsible for the magnetic properties of steel and cast iron, making it a classic example of a ferromagnetic material. In practical terms, ferrite can be considered nearly pure iron, with a tensile strength of approximately 280 N/mm². At room temperature, ferrite contains about 0.006% carbon. Low-carbon steels (up to 0.02 wt% carbon) are predominantly composed of ferrite. As the carbon content increases, the material develops increasing amounts of pearlite, which is a fine lamellar structure consisting of alternating layers of ferrite and cementite. Bainite and pearlite, both of which contain ferrite as a component, are common microstructures in iron-carbon alloys. Therefore, any iron-carbon alloy that is allowed to reach equilibrium at room temperature will contain some amount of ferrite. In pure iron, ferrite is stable at temperatures below 910°C. Above this temperature, the face-centered cubic (FCC) form of iron, known as austenite (gamma iron), becomes stable. At temperatures above 1390°C and up to the melting point of 1539°C, the body-centered cubic structure reappears as delta ferrite (δ-Fe), which is the more stable form at these high temperatures. The solubility of carbon in ferrite is limited because carbon atoms dissolve interstitially in the iron lattice. Carbon atoms are approximately twice the size of the interstitial spaces (holes) in the iron lattice, which creates a strong local strain field around each carbon atom. This results in a positive enthalpy of mixing, which is thermodynamically unfavorable. However, the entropy contribution to the free energy of the solution stabilizes the structure at low carbon concentrations. At 723°C, ferrite with a carbon content of approximately 0.02 wt% is stable. At this temperature, a eutectoid reaction occurs, involving ferrite, austenite, and cementite. This reaction is a critical transformation in the iron-carbon phase diagram, dictating the microstructural evolution of steel during cooling.
